# A strange rattling only when accelerating from 0 in cold weather

A rattling noise that triggers exclusively during cold starts, specifically upon applying throttle, points to a specific mechanical condition: thermal expansion and contraction affecting component clearance. In your 2005 Honda Civic, the symptom of a sound resembling a chain moving or trickling only during acceleration suggests that a part is momentarily loose or misaligned until engine heat warms the surrounding metal.

The most common culprit in this scenario is the timing chain tensioner or guide rails. While you have already replaced the timing belt, it is crucial to distinguish between a belt-driven system and a chain-driven one, as many Honda Civics from that era utilize a timing *chain* rather than a belt. If your vehicle actually uses a chain, replacing a belt was likely an unnecessary intervention unless the car was mistakenly identified or modified.

When the engine is cold, metal components contract. The timing chain tensioner relies on hydraulic pressure to maintain proper tension against this contraction. If the tensioner's piston sticks due to old oil viscosity or internal wear, it may not fully extend to take up slack when the engine is cold. Once you press the gas pedal, the crankshaft and camshafts rotate with increased torque, causing the chain to tighten slightly. Any slack created by the non-functioning tensioner results in the chain rattling against its guides or sprockets. As the engine warms up, the hydraulic fluid inside the tensioner thins, allowing it to extend further and eliminate the slack, which is why the noise disappears once you reach operating temperature.

Another possibility involves the intermediate shaft or idler pulleys that guide the chain. These components can develop play in their bearings over time. When cold, the metal housing contracts around a worn bearing, creating a tight fit that masks the rattle. Under load (acceleration), the slight movement of the shaft becomes audible as a clatter before thermal expansion loosens the fit or changes the friction dynamics.

It is also worth considering the accessory drive belts for the alternator, power steering pump, or A/C compressor. These belts are tensioned by idler pulleys and automatic tensioners that can seize when cold. If an idler pulley bearing fails, it might not make noise until the belt is under load. However, the description of a "chain" sound makes this less likely than a primary engine timing issue.

If your vehicle actually has a timing *belt* (which depends on the specific model year and engine code), ensure the replacement included new tensioners and water pump bearings, as these are wear items that fail independently of the belt itself. A failed tensioner in a belt system would exhibit identical symptoms: silence at idle, noise under load, and resolution after warming up.

To diagnose this without disassembly, listen closely to whether the sound originates from the front of the engine (timing cover area) or the accessory belt area. If the timing chain is indeed the issue, it is a critical repair because excessive slack can lead to valve-to-piston contact in interference engines. Do not ignore this symptom; waiting for the noise to become constant could indicate that the tensioner has completely collapsed or the chain has jumped teeth.
